metaDesc: A real-world guide to waterfalls and nature around Chiang Mai, Thailand — Huay Kaew close to town, the 10-tier Mae Sa Falls, Bua Tong Sticky Waterfall, San Kamphaeng Hot Springs, and the Mae Kampong forest trek, with fees, hours, and the best months for full water flow.

ogTitle: Chiang Mai Waterfalls & Nature — Where the Water Runs, How to Get There, What It Costs
ogDesc: Huay Kaew, Mae Sa, Bua Tong, San Kamphaeng Hot Springs, Mae Kampong trek — only the spots open for real, with locations and the best months for full flow.
intro: One of the best things about Chiang Mai is that you can drive half an hour out of town and already be standing in front of a waterfall surrounded by green forest. From Huay Kaew Falls right behind the zoo on the edge of the city, to Bua Tong where you climb the rock barefoot, to soaking your feet and boiling eggs at San Kamphaeng Hot Springs, or trekking up to the mountain village of Mae Kampong. We've picked only the places you can actually visit right now, and we'll tell you straight which months have plenty of water and which ones are so dry it isn't worth the trip.

blocks.html: Chiang Mai is ringed by mountains, so there are a lot of waterfalls here — from easy, kid-friendly walks to ones where you have to push through a bit of forest. The most important thing to know is the season. Most waterfalls run full from late rainy season into early winter (July–December), while in the hot months (March–May) some dry up to little more than rocks and a few small pools. We'll tell you when to go for each one.

blocks.text: Waterfalls Near Town — Easy to Reach, No Long Drive

blocks.html: If you only have half a day or don't feel like a long drive, these three are along the Doi Suthep–Mae Rim side, between 30 minutes and an hour from the city center.

items.name: Huay Kaew Waterfall
items.blurb: The closest waterfall to town, at the foot of Doi Suthep behind Chiang Mai Zoo, near the Kruba Srivichai monument. It's just a few minutes' walk from the parking area, so it's an easy stop before heading up Doi Suthep. The falls aren't huge, but it's shady and green, and locals come to hang out here.
items.meta: ~6 km from town · open 08:00–17:00 · free entry

items.name: Monthathan Waterfall (Mon Tha Than)
items.blurb: A 9-tier waterfall inside Doi Suthep–Pui National Park, on the same road up to Doi Suthep. Clear water drops into pools, and it's shadier and quieter than Huay Kaew — good if you like a gentle forest walk. In the dry season (Jan–May) the water drops off a lot, so aim for late rainy season.
items.meta: Inside Doi Suthep–Pui Park · open 08:30–16:30 · foreigners 100 THB, Thais 20 THB + vehicle fee

items.name: Mae Sa Waterfall
items.blurb: A 10-tier waterfall in Doi Suthep–Pui National Park on the Mae Rim side, about 30 minutes to an hour from town. A wooden walkway runs alongside the falls so you can climb tier by tier — doing all 10 takes about an hour each way. You can swim in the lower tiers, and there are picnic areas, so it works well for families.
items.meta: Mae Rim district ~30 km · foreigners 100 THB, Thais 20 THB + vehicle fee ~30 THB

blocks.title: About National Park Entry Fees
blocks.html: Waterfalls inside national parks (Mae Sa, Monthathan) charge separate rates for Thais and foreigners — foreign adults around 100 THB, children 50 THB, Thai adults 20 THB, plus a vehicle fee of about 30 THB per car. Prices can change, so bring cash just in case.

blocks.text: Bua Tong — The Waterfall You Climb Barefoot

blocks.html: If you had to pick one of the most unusual waterfalls around Chiang Mai, it would be Bua Tong, which many people call the "Sticky Waterfall." It's in Mae Taeng district, about 60 kilometers from the old town — roughly an hour and a half by car.

What makes it special is that the rock here is coated in limestone (calcium carbonate), giving the surface a rough, sponge-like texture that doesn't get slippery underfoot. So you can climb straight up against the flow of the water barefoot, with ropes along the side to grab at intervals. Kids and older folks can manage it too, as long as they take it slow.

items: Free entry, open daily 08:00–17:00, with parking and restrooms.
Barefoot is best — sandals tend to be slipperier, so just leave them at the bottom.
Watch out for the green patches where there's algae on the rock — those spots are slippery and don't grip like the brown rock, so avoid them.
At the top there's the Chet Si (Seven-Color) Spring (Huay Tad Spring), where the source water bubbles up from underground — you can keep walking past the top of the falls to reach it.

blocks.title: When to Go to Bua Tong
blocks.html: The rock grips best when the water isn't running too hard. Early winter (Nov–Feb) is the sweet spot — the flow is just right and the weather is cool and pleasant. In the rainy season the water runs harder and the rock is slipperier, so you have to be more careful climbing.

blocks.text: San Kamphaeng Hot Springs — Soak Your Feet, Boil Eggs

blocks.html: Heading east out of town about 35 kilometers, around Mae On district, you'll find the San Kamphaeng Hot Springs, a natural hot spring that shoots up in a tall jet. People come to soak their feet in the warm channels and buy a basket of eggs to lower into the boiling pools — wait a few minutes and you've got freshly cooked eggs to eat on the spot.

items: Open daily ~07:00–19:00, entry around 100 THB for foreigners and around 40 THB for Thais.
Private mineral baths available for an extra charge per person — good if you want a proper soak, not just a foot dip.
Eggs are sold by the basket near the pools, with signs showing cooking times for each style — soft-boiled with a runny yolk takes about 7 minutes.
Pairs well with a trip around the San Kamphaeng–Mae On side, like adding Mae Kampong in the same day.

blocks.html: If you want nature that goes deeper than a roadside waterfall, Chiang Mai has mountain villages with real trekking trails, where the air stays cool and pleasant because of the altitude.

items.name: Mae Kampong Village
items.blurb: A village in the forest at about 1,300 meters in Mae On district, roughly an hour's drive from town. It has the 7-tier Mae Kampong Waterfall, about a 30-minute walk up from the village. The village grows miang (fermented tea leaf), tea, and coffee, and there are cafes tucked in the forest to relax at. The air stays cool all year.

items.name: Doi Suthep–Pui Park (Trekking Trails)
items.blurb: Beyond the temple and the waterfalls, there are nature-study trails through the forest, good for people who want a gentle walk close to town. They start around Monthathan or behind Chiang Mai University.

blocks.title: If You Want Serious Trekking
blocks.html: For deeper-forest trekking, like the Mae Kampong route or inside the park, we'd hire a local guide. Some stretches of trail aren't signposted, and the paths get slippery in the rainy season. A guide knows where the hidden waterfalls are and helps with safety.

If you have a car and two days, this is a route that covers the nature around Chiang Mai without wearing you out — splitting the west side (Doi Suthep–Mae Rim) and the east side (San Kamphaeng–Mae On) across two days.

items: Check the season — water is fullest July–December. In the hot season some waterfalls dry up, so if you come then, pick Bua Tong or the hot springs, which don't depend on rain.
Bring cash — park entry and the hot springs mostly take cash only.
Shoes and clothes you don't mind getting wet, especially for Bua Tong and Mae Sa — bring a spare set.
Rent a car or motorbike — most spots have no public transport to the waterfall itself. A sedan runs about 1,000 THB a day, a motorbike about 200–300 THB, or you can charter a songthaew.
Slippery in the rainy season — especially the waterfall rocks and the roads up the mountains, so drive and walk carefully.

faq.q: Which Chiang Mai waterfall has the most water, and when should I go?
faq.a: Most waterfalls run full from late rainy season into early winter — July through December. In the hot season (March–May), many run low or dry up. If you're coming in the hot season, go for Bua Tong (the Sticky Waterfall) or the hot springs, which don't depend much on rain.

faq.q: What's the closest waterfall to Chiang Mai city?
faq.a: Huay Kaew Waterfall, at the foot of Doi Suthep behind Chiang Mai Zoo, about 6 kilometers from town. It's free, open roughly 08:00–17:00, and just a few minutes' walk from the parking area — a good stop before heading up Doi Suthep.

faq.q: Can you really climb Bua Tong Waterfall? Is it dangerous?
faq.a: Yes, you can really climb it, because the limestone coating makes the rock rough and non-slip. We'd recommend climbing barefoot and grabbing the ropes along the side. Avoid the spots with green algae, since those are slippery. Kids and older people can do it if they're careful and have someone helping watch.

faq.q: Is San Kamphaeng Hot Springs free? What can you do there?
faq.a: There's an entry fee — around 100 THB for foreigners and around 40 THB for Thais — open roughly 07:00–19:00. You can soak your feet in the warm channels, buy eggs to boil in the hot pools, or pay extra for a private mineral bath.

faq.q: Do I need my own vehicle to visit the waterfalls around Chiang Mai?
faq.a: Almost none of them have public transport to the waterfall itself. The easiest option is to rent a car or motorbike — motorbikes run about 200–300 THB a day, sedans from around 1,000 THB a day — or you can charter a songthaew or book a day tour.
